meta.title: Finding Similar Items at Scale — Part 1
meta.subtitle: Entity resolution, and the similarity and distance measures that decide it
meta.summary: The same real-world entity turns up under countless descriptions, and one description can name many entities. This first part defines entity resolution, shows at which levels it happens, and builds the toolbox for deciding it: string similarity for atomic values, Jaccard similarity for sets, and the distance measures — Euclidean and non-Euclidean — used everywhere after. It ends with the deduplication pipeline and the quadratic cost that Parts 2 and 3 set out to beat.
objectives: Define entity resolution, explain why one entity gets many descriptions, and list the steps of the typical methodology.
Name the levels at which entity resolution happens and the four families of solutions.
Compute edit, gap and Jaro similarity for short strings and say which suits which case.
Compute Jaccard similarity and Jaccard distance of two sets.
State the four axioms of a distance measure and tell Euclidean from non-Euclidean spaces.
Compute L₁, L₂, L∞, cosine and Hamming distances, and pick a measure that fits the data.
Trace the deduplication pipeline from pairwise similarity to a clean relation, and explain why comparing all pairs does not scale.
takeaways: Entity resolution decides whether two data structures correspond to the same real-world entity: identify them, decide how to merge, update the collection.
Descriptions diverge through text variations (misspellings, acronyms, abbreviations…) and local knowledge (own formats, no global identifier coordination).
Solutions work at four levels: atomic values, sets, inner relationships and uncertain data.
Edit distance counts inserts, deletes and updates; gap distance makes abbreviations cheap; Jaro and Jaro-Winkler suit short names.
Jaccard similarity is |C₁ ∩ C₂| / |C₁ ∪ C₂|; Jaccard distance is one minus it.
A distance measure is non-negative, zero exactly for identical points, symmetric, and obeys the triangle inequality.
Euclidean spaces have the Lᵣ norms — L₂, L₁ (Manhattan), L∞; non-Euclidean measures include Jaccard, cosine, edit and Hamming distance.
Deduplication scores pairs, clusters similar records and merges each cluster — but N records give N(N−1)/2 pairs, which Parts 2 and 3 avoid.

concepts.short: Deciding whether two data structures describe the same real-world entity.
concepts.detail: The methodology has three parts: identify the data that describes the same object, decide how to merge it, and update the data collection. It travels under many names — record linkage, deduplication, entity matching, merge/purge, reference reconciliation, object identification, duplicate detection.

concepts.short: Text variations plus local knowledge produce many names for one entity.
concepts.detail: Text variations cover misspellings, acronyms, transformations and abbreviations. Local knowledge is the deeper cause: every source picks its own format (a person as the author of a publication is not described like a person in an email), and nobody coordinates identifier assignment globally.

concepts.short: Atomic similarity, similarity for sets, inner relationships, and methods for uncertain data.
concepts.detail: They correspond to the level at which two descriptions are compared: single values such as names, sets of values such as co-authors, the relationships connecting a record to others, and data whose values are themselves uncertain.

concepts.short: The cheapest sequence of character edits that turns one string into another.
concepts.detail: In the Levenshtein formulation, delete, insert and update each cost 1 — turning *ekaterini* into *katerina* costs 2. The book uses an insert/delete-only variant, where $d(x,y) = |x| + |y| - 2 \cdot |LCS(x,y)|$. Both are proper distance measures.

concepts.short: Edit distance plus cheap 'open gap' and 'extend gap' operations.
concepts.detail: Plain edit distance punishes abbreviations badly: turning 'knowledge and data' into 'knowl. data' costs one edit per deleted character. Charging once to open a gap and a small amount $e$ per extension makes that cost $1 + o + 8e$.

concepts.short: A similarity tuned for short strings such as first and last names.
concepts.detail: With $C$ common characters and $T$ transpositions (half the number of mismatched common characters), $Jaro(s_1,s_2) = \frac{1}{3}\left(\frac{C}{|s_1|} + \frac{C}{|s_2|} + \frac{C-T}{C}\right)$. Jaro-Winkler adds extra weight for a matching prefix, which suits personal names.

concepts.short: Intersection over union; distance is one minus the similarity.
concepts.detail: $SIM(C_1,C_2) = \frac{|C_1 \cap C_2|}{|C_1 \cup C_2|}$ and $d(C_1,C_2) = 1 - SIM(C_1,C_2)$. It compares sets of values — the co-authors of two publications, the words or shingles of two documents, the products two customers bought.

concepts.short: Non-negative, zero exactly for identical points, symmetric, and obeys the triangle inequality.
concepts.detail: $d(x,y) \ge 0$; $d(x,y) = 0$ iff $x = y$; $d(x,y) = d(y,x)$; $d(x,y) \le d(x,z) + d(z,y)$. Jaccard, edit, Hamming, cosine and all Lᵣ distances qualify.

concepts.short: In a space of real-valued dimensions: L₂ (straight line), L₁ (Manhattan), L∞ (largest difference).
concepts.detail: $L_r(x,y) = \left(\sum_i |x_i - y_i|^r\right)^{1/r}$. $L_2$ is the most common notion of distance, $L_1$ is the distance travelled along the coordinates, and $L_\infty$ — the limit as $r \to \infty$ — is the maximum difference in any dimension. For $a = (5,5)$ and $b = (9,8)$: $L_2 = 5$, $L_1 = 7$, $L_\infty = 4$.

concepts.short: Jaccard for sets, cosine for vectors, edit for strings, Hamming for bit vectors.
concepts.detail: They depend on properties of the points rather than their location in a space — there is no meaningful *average* of two sets or two strings. Cosine distance is the angle $\arccos\frac{x \cdot y}{\|x\|\|y\|}$, between 0° and 180°; Hamming distance counts the positions in which two vectors differ.

concepts.short: Compute pairwise similarity, cluster similar records, merge each cluster into one unified record.
concepts.detail: Clustering closes matches transitively, so a threshold that looks safe pair by pair can still chain different entities together. The merge rule decides per field which value survives — majority, most recent, or an aggregate.

quiz.prompt: Which of these is a case of *local knowledge*, rather than a text variation, causing two descriptions of one entity?

options.text: “Trans. Knowl. Data Eng.” abbreviating a journal name.
One source stores a person as a publication author, another as an email sender, each with its own format and identifiers.

quiz.explanation: Abbreviations, misspellings and acronyms are **text variations**. **Local knowledge** is the deeper cause: each source picks its own format, and there is no global coordination for identifier assignment.

quiz.prompt: Co-author lists separate the different researchers called “Ling Chen” on DBLP. Which family of solutions is that?
quiz.explanation: The name string is identical, so no atomic similarity can tell the authors apart. Comparing the **sets** of co-authors (and venues) of two publications can: papers sharing co-authors such as Sourav S. Bhowmick belong to the same Ling Chen.

quiz.prompt: With insert, delete and update each costing 1, what is the edit distance between “ekaterini” and “katerina”?
quiz.explanation: Delete the leading *e* and update the final *i* into *a*: two operations. (Drawn the other way round, it is an insert and an update.)

quiz.prompt: What is the Jaro similarity of DEIS and DESI?
quiz.explanation: All $C = 4$ characters are common; *I* and *S* appear in swapped order, two mismatched positions, so $T = 2/2 = 1$. $Jaro = \frac{1}{3}\left(\frac{4}{4} + \frac{4}{4} + \frac{4-1}{4}\right) = \frac{2.75}{3} \approx 0.9167$.

quiz.prompt: Encoded as bit vectors, C₁ = 10111 and C₂ = 10011. What is their Jaccard distance?
quiz.explanation: Intersection (bitwise AND) has 3 ones, union (bitwise OR) has 4, so the Jaccard similarity is $3/4$ and the distance is $1 - 3/4 = 1/4$.

quiz.prompt: Which of these is NOT one of the four axioms of a distance measure?

options.text: d(x, y) ≤ d(x, z) + d(z, y)

quiz.explanation: The axioms are non-negativity, $d(x,y) = 0$ exactly when $x = y$, symmetry, and the triangle inequality. Nothing bounds a distance by 1 — Euclidean and edit distances grow without limit.

quiz.prompt: For a = (5, 5) and b = (9, 8), what are the L₂, L₁ and L∞ distances?
quiz.explanation: The differences are 4 and 3. $L_2 = \sqrt{4^2 + 3^2} = 5$, $L_1 = 4 + 3 = 7$ (the Manhattan route along the axes), and $L_\infty = \max(4, 3) = 4$.

quiz.prompt: What is the cosine distance between [1, 2, −1] and [2, 1, 1]?
quiz.explanation: The dot product is $2 + 2 - 1 = 3$ and both vectors have length $\sqrt{6}$, so $\cos\theta = 3/6 = 1/2$ and $\theta = 60°$.

quiz.prompt: You want to compare customers by the sets of products they bought. Which distance fits best?
quiz.explanation: The data are sets, so Jaccard distance applies directly. Edit distance and Jaro are for strings; $L_2$ needs real-valued coordinates — there is no meaningful location of a set in a space.

quiz.prompt: Why are sets and strings said to live in non-Euclidean spaces?

options.text: Because their distances violate the triangle inequality.
Because there is no notion of the average of two points — distances depend on properties of the points, not on a location.
Because they have infinitely many dimensions.
Because their distances are always between 0 and 1.

quiz.explanation: A Euclidean space has real-valued dimensions and dense points, so you can average two points. There is no average of two sets or two strings; their distance measures are still proper distances, just not based on location.

quiz.prompt: Deduplication accepts every pair scoring at least 0.6. P1–P2 scores 0.9 and P2–P5 scores 0.6, but P1–P5 was never compared. Where does P5 end up?

options.text: In its own cluster, since it was not compared with P1.
In the same cluster as P1 and P2, because clustering closes matches transitively.
It is deleted as a duplicate of P2.
It depends on the merge rule.

quiz.explanation: Clustering connects records through chains of accepted pairs, so P1, P2 and P5 form one cluster and are merged into one unified record. That is why the clusters a threshold produces need checking, not just the pairs.

quiz.prompt: You must deduplicate one million records. Why is scoring every pair with a good similarity function not an option?

options.text: The similarity function itself is too inaccurate at that scale.
There are about 5 × 10¹¹ pairs, which takes days even at a million comparisons per second.
One million records cannot fit in main memory.
Jaccard similarity is undefined for more than 1000 sets.

quiz.explanation: $N(N-1)/2 \approx 5 \times 10^{11}$ pairs. At $10^6$ comparisons per second and $10^5$ seconds per day that is about five days — and ten million records take more than a year. That cost is the *problem for the next lecture*.

blocks.md: *Finding Similar Items at Scale* runs over three lectures with one body of study material, built on chapter 3 of *Mining of Massive Datasets* (§3.1.1–§3.4, §3.5 and §3.8.1–§3.8.3). This first part is about entity resolution: what the problem is, why it is unavoidable, at which levels it occurs, and which similarity and distance measures decide it — with their formulas and the situations they suit.

blocks.md:
How many names and descriptions are used for the same real-world entity? Start with a single city. *London* is written as Londres, Londra, Londyn, Lontoo, Lunnainn, ロンドン, Лондон, 伦敦 and a hundred other strings. It is also described as *the capital of the UK*, *the host city of the IV and XIV Olympic Games*, *the city of the Westminster Abbey*, *the city of the London Eye*, *the city described by Charles Dickens in his novels* — and identified by URIs on GeoNames, Wikipedia and DBpedia. One entity, unbounded descriptions.

Now run it the other way: how many entities have the same name? A gazetteer lists London KY, London OH, London AR, London TX, London MO, London MI, London in Conecuh County AL and dozens more — and a phone book lists *Jack London* in Montgomery AL at two addresses with the same phone number, another in Van Buren AR, another in La Jolla CA. One string, many entities.

blocks.title: The definition, in one line
blocks.md: **Entity resolution** is deciding whether two data structures correspond to the same real-world entity. Everything else in these three lectures is about making that decision well — and cheaply enough to be useful at scale.

rows: Each source uses different formats — a person from a publication is not described like a person from an email — and there is no global coordination for identifier assignment.
blocks.caption: Reasons for various descriptions of the same entity.

blocks.title: The required process
blocks.intro: The typical entity-resolution methodology has three steps, whatever technique implements them.

steps.title: Identify
steps.md: Find the data describing the same real-world objects.

steps.title: Decide how to merge
steps.md: Choose how the matching descriptions are combined into one.

steps.title: Update the data collection
steps.md: Replace the duplicates by the merged result.

blocks.md: Because the problem appears everywhere, it has many names: record linkage, entity linkage, deduplication, duplicate detection, merge/purge, entity matching, reference reconciliation, object identification, data cleaning, fuzzy matching. When you meet any of them in a paper or a tool, it is this problem.

cards.answer: Deciding whether two data structures correspond to the same real-world entity.

cards.prompt: What are the two reasons descriptions of one entity diverge?
cards.answer: Text variations (misspellings, acronyms, transformations, abbreviations) and local knowledge (each source has its own format; no global identifier coordination).

cards.prompt: What are the three steps of the typical methodology?
cards.answer: Identify the data describing the same real-world objects, decide how to merge it, update the data collection.

blocks.md: Solutions to entity resolution follow various directions. They fall into **four categories**, which also tell you at which **level** two descriptions are being compared:

rows: Single values — one string against another
“John D. Smith” vs. “J. D. Smith”; journal names and their abbreviations
Sets of values attached to each description
The co-authors of two publications, the words of two documents
Two author records are likelier the same person when they link to the same co-authors and venues
Values that are themselves uncertain or probabilistic
Matching must reason with probabilities rather than exact values

blocks.md:
In practice the data structures being compared are usually **records**, and records combine all of these levels. Take two customer records:

- *Jonathan Smith*, age 43, born `17/05/1983`, `12 Baker St.`, London `NW1 6XE`, `United Kingdom`, phone `07700 900123`, `jsmith@gmail.com`, Senior Software Developer at *Acme Corporation*, income 78,500, 3 children, customer id `UK-88219`.
- *John Smith*, age 42, born `1983-05-17`, `12 Baker Street`, London `NW1 6XE`, `UK`, phone `+44 7700 900123`, `john.smith@gmail.com`, Software Engineer at *Acme Ltd.*, income 72,000, married, 2 children, customer id `C104582`.

Almost every field differs — yet the date of birth, address, postcode and phone are the same values in different **formats**, which is local knowledge at work. A second pair shows the harder case of **sparse** records with different attributes: one has a phone number and an occupation, the other an email and an employer, and only name, age, city and postcode can be compared directly.

blocks.title: Records are compared field by field
blocks.md: A record matcher applies an atomic similarity to each comparable field — Jaro for first names, edit distance for addresses, exact match for postcodes — and combines the field scores into one decision. The other levels add evidence the fields alone cannot: shared sets of values and shared relationships.

cards.prompt: Name the four categories of entity-resolution solutions.
cards.answer: Atomic similarity methods, similarity methods for sets, facilitating inner-relationships, methods in uncertain data.

cards.prompt: Why are “17/05/1983” and “1983-05-17” a problem, and which reason for diverging descriptions is it?
cards.answer: The same value in different formats defeats exact comparison — local knowledge (each source uses its own format).

cards.prompt: What makes the second pair of Smith records harder than the first?
cards.answer: They are sparse and have different attributes, so only a few fields (name, age, city, postcode) can be compared directly.

blocks.md:
The first family compares field values directly. Two classic targets: publication authors, where *John D. Smith* must match *J. D. Smith*, and journal names, where *Transactions on Knowledge and Data Engineering* must match *Trans. Knowl. Data Eng.*

**Edit distance** is the number of operations needed to convert the first string into the second. In the Levenshtein distance [Lev66], delete, insert and update a character each cost 1. Turning *ekaterini* into *katerina* costs 2: remove the leading *e* and update the final *i* into *a*.

blocks.title: Edit distance punishes abbreviation
blocks.md: Shortening *knowledge and data* to *knowl. data* costs one edit per deleted character. **Gap distance** [Nav01] overcomes this limitation with two extra operations — **open gap**, and **extend gap** at a small cost — so the total becomes $1 + o + 8e$: one insert for the dot, one gap opening, eight cheap extensions.

For short strings such as first and last names, **Jaro similarity** works better. It counts the characters $C$ that the two strings have in common and the transpositions $T$ — half the number of positions $k$ where both strings have a common character but $s_1[k] \ne s_2[k]$.

blocks.caption: For DEIS versus DESI: C = 4, T = 2/2 = 1, giving (4/4 + 4/4 + 3/4)/3 = 0.9167.

blocks.md: **Jaro-Winkler similarity** extends Jaro by giving a matching **prefix** higher weight, which increases its applicability to names — people rarely misspell the first letters of a name.

blocks.title: String similarity lab
blocks.description: Compare the measures on the same pair of strings, and watch the dynamic-programming table that produces the edit distance.

blocks.title: Two definitions of edit distance
blocks.md: The Levenshtein edit distance allows insert, delete **and** update. The book (§3.5.5) uses insert and delete only, which makes $d(x,y) = |x| + |y| - 2|LCS(x,y)|$ with LCS the longest common subsequence. For *abcde* and *acfdeg* the LCS is *acde*, so the distance is $5 + 6 - 8 = 3$. Both versions are distance measures; know which one a question means.

tasks.prompt: Using the book's insert/delete edit distance, what is $d(x, y)$ for $x = abcde$ and $y = acfdeg$?
tasks.solution: The longest common subsequence is *acde* (length 4), so $d = 5 + 6 - 2 \cdot 4 = $ **3**: delete *b*, insert *f* after *c*, insert *g* at the end.

tasks.prompt: Compute the Jaro similarity of MARTHA and MARHTA, to three decimals.
tasks.hint: All six characters are common; *T* and *H* are swapped.
tasks.solution: $C = 6$; the mismatched positions are those of T and H, two of them, so $T = 2/2 = 1$. $Jaro = \frac{1}{3}(6/6 + 6/6 + 5/6) = $ **0.944**.

blocks.md: Atomic similarity fails when the strings are **identical** but the entities are not. DBLP lists dozens of publications by *Ling Chen* — and they belong to several different researchers. The name cannot separate them; the **sets** around each publication can. Papers co-authored with Sourav S. Bhowmick match each other; papers with Henry Y. H. Chuang form another group; papers with Yunjun Gao, Chun Li and Gencai Chen another. Comparing sets of co-authors (and venues) is the second family of solutions.
The natural measure for sets is **Jaccard similarity**: the size of their intersection divided by the size of their union.

blocks.tex: SIM(C_1, C_2) = \frac{|C_1 \cap C_2|}{|C_1 \cup C_2|} \qquad d(C_1, C_2) = 1 - SIM(C_1, C_2)
blocks.caption: Jaccard similarity and Jaccard distance (MMDS §3.1.1). Two sets with 3 elements in their intersection and 8 in their union have similarity 3/8.

tasks.prompt: What is the Jaccard similarity of {1, 2, 3, 4} and {2, 3, 5, 7}?
Paper A has co-authors {Bhowmick, Nejdl}, paper B has {Bhowmick, Li}. What is the Jaccard **distance** between the co-author sets?
tasks.solution: Similarity = 1/3 (one shared co-author out of three distinct ones), so the distance is $1 - 1/3 = $ **2/3**.

blocks.md: Every similarity above can be turned into a **distance**, and the rest of the course relies on distances obeying a few rules. $d$ is a **distance measure** if it is a function from pairs of points to real numbers such that:

blocks.tex: d(x,y) \ge 0 \qquad d(x,y) = 0 \iff x = y \qquad d(x,y) = d(y,x) \qquad d(x,y) \le d(x,z) + d(z,y)
blocks.caption: Non-negativity, identity, symmetry, and the triangle inequality: no detour through z is shorter than the direct route.

blocks.md: A **Euclidean space** has some number of real-valued dimensions and “dense” points: there is a notion of the **average** of two points, and a Euclidean distance is based on the **locations** of points in the space. Any other space is **non-Euclidean**: its distance measures are based on properties of the points, not on their location — there is no average of two sets or of two strings.

blocks.tex: L_r(x, y) = \Big(\sum_{i=1}^{n} |x_i - y_i|^r\Big)^{1/r} \qquad L_\infty(x, y) = \max_i |x_i - y_i|
blocks.caption: The Lᵣ norm: take the r-th power of the differences, sum, take the r-th root. L∞ is the limit as r goes to infinity.

rows: Square root of the sum of the squared differences in each dimension — the most common notion of distance
Sum of the absolute differences in each dimension — the distance if you had to travel along the coordinates only
The maximum of the differences in any dimension
blocks.caption: Examples of Euclidean distances for a = (5, 5) and b = (9, 8).

rows: The angle between the vectors, arccos(x·y / ‖x‖‖y‖), from 0° to 180°
Number of inserts and deletes to change one string into the other
Number of positions in which they differ
blocks.caption: Non-Euclidean distances. Cosine distance also works in Euclidean spaces, but there it ignores the length of the vectors.

blocks.title: Distance explorer
blocks.description: Type two vectors and compare every measure at once. Two-dimensional vectors are drawn with their L₂ line and L₁ route.

blocks.title: Why each measure really is a distance (MMDS §3.5)

steps.title: Lᵣ norms
steps.md: Absolute values make them non-negative and symmetric, they are zero only when every coordinate agrees, and the triangle inequality holds — for $L_2$ it is the familiar fact that one side of a triangle is never longer than the other two.

steps.title: Jaccard distance
steps.md:
$1 - SIM$ is between 0 and 1, zero only for identical sets ($x \cup x = x \cap x$), and symmetric. The triangle inequality follows from minhashing (Part 2): $d(x,y)$ is the probability that a random minhash function gives $h(x) 
e h(y)$, and whenever that happens, $h(x) 
e h(z)$ or $h(z) 
e h(y)$ must hold — so $d(x,y) \le d(x,z) + d(z,y)$.

steps.title: Cosine distance
steps.md: Angles lie between 0° and 180°, two vectors have angle 0 only if they point the same way (treat multiples of a vector as the same point), and rotating from $x$ to $z$ to $y$ is never shorter than rotating from $x$ to $y$ directly.

steps.title: Edit distance
steps.md: Only identical strings need zero edits, every edit sequence can be reversed (symmetry), and turning $x$ into $z$ then $z$ into $y$ is one valid way to turn $x$ into $y$, so the direct cost is no higher.

steps.title: Hamming distance
steps.md: It counts differing components, so it is non-negative, symmetric and zero only for identical vectors; any component where $x$ and $y$ differ must differ between $x$ and $z$ or between $z$ and $y$.

rows: Typos and small changes in longer strings (addresses, titles)
Short strings such as first and last names
Sets of values: co-authors, shingles, products bought
Vectors where direction matters more than magnitude (e.g. word-count vectors of documents)
L₂, or L₁ when movement is along axes, L∞ when the worst dimension matters
blocks.caption: Which measure to choose.

tasks.prompt: What is the Hamming distance between 10101 and 11110?
tasks.solution: They differ in the second, fourth and fifth positions: **3**.

tasks.prompt: For x = (1, 2, 3) and y = (4, 6, 3), give the L₁ distance.
Which of these are non-Euclidean distance measures? Select all that apply.
tasks.solution: **Jaccard**, **edit** and **Hamming** distance are defined on sets, strings and bit vectors, which have no locations to average. The Lᵣ norms are the Euclidean distances. (Cosine distance is sometimes listed among both.)

blocks.md: **Entity linkage and deduplication** identifies the different representations of the same real-world entity and merges them into **one unified record** — four inconsistently formatted part records (O-Ring Gasket, 27-00091, in four layouts) become one. Applied to a relation with duplicates it is a three-step pipeline:

items.label: Step 1
items.title: Compute pairwise similarity
items.md: Score pairs of records: P3–P4 at 1.0, P1–P2 at 0.9, P2–P5 at 0.5, P1–P5 at 0.3; P6 is similar to nobody.

items.label: Step 2
items.title: Cluster similar records
items.md: Group records whose similarity clears a threshold: {P1, P2, P5}, {P3, P4}, {P6}.

items.label: Step 3
items.title: Merge clusters
items.md: Produce one record per cluster — the clean relation C1 (Green, 51519), C2 (Peter, 30528), C3 (Chuck, 51519).

blocks.caption: A relation with duplicates (example by Ihab Ilyas). The clean relation has three records: Green 51519 39k, Peter 30528 40k, Chuck 51519 30k.

blocks.title: Threshold, clusters and the clean relation
blocks.description: Six records, seven scored pairs. Move the threshold and watch clusters form by transitive closure — and the merged relation change with them.

blocks.title: Clustering is transitive
blocks.md: If $P_1$ matches $P_2$ and $P_2$ matches $P_5$, all three end up in one entity — even if $P_1$ and $P_5$ were never compared, or compared badly. A threshold that looks safe pair by pair can chain two different entities together.

cards.prompt: What are the three steps of deduplication?
cards.answer: Compute pairwise similarity, cluster similar records, merge clusters into unified records.

cards.prompt: In the example, why does P5 (Gree, 51519, 55k) join the Green cluster?
cards.answer: Its similarity to P1 (and P2) clears the threshold — *Gree* is one edit from *Green* and the ZIP matches — and clustering closes matches transitively.

blocks.md: What does entity linkage cost? Every pair of records must, in principle, be scored — and the number of pairs grows quadratically.

blocks.title: The quadratic wall
blocks.description: Before any clever technique, see what brute force costs. Move the sliders and watch the wall arrive.

blocks.title: Blocking and hashing
blocks.md: The way out is the idea behind every hash index: hash each item into a **bucket** and only compare items that land in the same bucket. Done naively — hashing on an exact field value — this is **blocking**, and it misses matches that disagree on the hashed field. Parts 2 and 3 build hash functions that put *similar* items into the same bucket on purpose.

blocks.title: Problem for the next lecture
blocks.md: **Given** high-dimensional data points $x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_N$ — an image, for example, is a long vector of pixel colours — **and** a distance function $d(x_i, x_j)$, **find** all pairs of data points within some distance threshold $d(x_i, x_j) \le s$. The naïve solution takes $O(N^2)$ time, where $N$ is the number of data points.

cards.prompt: How many pairs do N records have, and how long does N = 10⁶ take at 10⁶ comparisons per second?
cards.answer: N(N−1)/2 ≈ 5 × 10¹¹ pairs — about 5 days at 10⁵ seconds per day; 10⁷ records take more than a year.

cards.prompt: Name three applications of finding similar sets.
cards.answer: E.g. near-duplicate or mirror pages, plagiarism, clustering news by story, customers with similar purchases, movies with similar fans, entity resolution.

cards.prompt: State the problem for the next lecture.
cards.answer: Given N high-dimensional points and a distance function, find all pairs within a distance threshold — without the naïve O(N²) comparison of all pairs.

blocks.title: Confusing similarity with distance
blocks.md: Jaccard **similarity** is intersection over union; Jaccard **distance** is one minus that. Read whether a question asks for $SIM$ or $d$ before answering.

blocks.title: Mixing up the two edit distances
blocks.md: With updates allowed (Levenshtein), changing one character costs 1. With inserts and deletes only (the book), it costs 2. Check which definition is in play.

blocks.title: Using a string measure on the wrong strings
blocks.md: Plain edit distance makes an abbreviation look far from its full form; Jaro rewards short names but means little on long addresses. Match the measure to the field.

blocks.title: Thinking a large L₂ means a large cosine distance
blocks.md: Cosine distance ignores vector length: [1, 1] and [10, 10] are 0° apart but far apart in $L_2$. Choose cosine when direction is what matters.

blocks.title: Forgetting that clustering is transitive
blocks.md: A threshold that looks safe pairwise can merge two clearly different entities through a chain of intermediate records. Always look at the clusters the threshold produces, not just at the pairs it accepts.
Twelve questions covering entity resolution, its measures and its cost. Read every explanation — the formulas in them are exactly what the exam asks you to apply.

items: Entity resolution decides whether two data structures correspond to the same real-world entity: identify them, decide how to merge, update the collection.
Descriptions diverge through text variations (misspellings, acronyms, abbreviations…) and local knowledge (own formats, no global identifier coordination).
Solutions work at four levels: atomic values, sets, inner relationships and uncertain data.
Edit distance counts inserts, deletes and updates; gap distance makes abbreviations cheap; Jaro and Jaro-Winkler suit short names.
Jaccard similarity is |C₁ ∩ C₂| / |C₁ ∪ C₂|; Jaccard distance is one minus it.
A distance measure is non-negative, zero exactly for identical points, symmetric, and obeys the triangle inequality.
Euclidean spaces have the Lᵣ norms — L₂, L₁ (Manhattan), L∞; non-Euclidean measures include Jaccard, cosine, edit and Hamming distance.
Deduplication scores pairs, clusters similar records and merges each cluster — but N records give N(N−1)/2 pairs, which Parts 2 and 3 avoid.

blocks.title: The one sentence version
blocks.md: Entity resolution decides whether two descriptions are the same entity by comparing values, sets, relationships or uncertain data with a suitable distance measure — and doing that for every pair is exactly what does not scale.
